tasks.intro: Here's how to undo a commit in Git, depending on whether it has been pushed.
tasks.notes: The safe rule: never rewrite history that has been pushed. `git reset` rewrites history (use it only locally); `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes the changes (safe to push).

languages.bash:
# ── Not pushed yet — safe to rewrite history ──────────────────
# Undo the last commit but KEEP the changes staged:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo the last commit and keep changes in the working tree (unstaged):
git reset --mixed HEAD~1      # this is the default for `git reset HEAD~1`

# Undo the last commit and DISCARD the changes entirely:
git reset --hard HEAD~1       # ⚠️ destructive — unrecoverable without reflog

# ── Already pushed — never rewrite shared history ──────────────────
# Add a new commit that reverses the last commit (safe to push):
git revert HEAD

# Revert a specific commit by hash:
git revert <commit-hash>

# ── Fix just the message of the last commit ─────────────────────────
git commit --amend -m "new message"

# ── Oops, forgot a file in the last commit ─────────────────────────
git add forgotten-file.txt
git commit --amend --no-edit

# Anything lost? Check the reflog — it records every HEAD move for ~90 days:
git reflog

# Discard unstaged changes (working tree only):
git checkout -- file.txt      # one file
git checkout -- .             # everything unstaged
git restore file.txt          # modern equivalent

# Unstage (keep changes): 
git reset HEAD file.txt

tasks.intro: Here's the standard Git workflow for committing changes.
tasks.notes: Commit small, focused changes with a clear message, and commit early and often. `git status` and `git diff` before staging prevent accidentally committing debugging leftovers.

languages.bash:
# See what changed before committing:
git status
git diff

# Stage specific files (or `git add .` for everything):
git add src/main.py tests/test_main.py

# Commit with a message (imperative mood, under 50 chars is a good habit):
git commit -m "Fix null pointer in user lookup"

# Verify:
git log --oneline -5

tasks.intro: Here's how to work with branches in Git.
tasks.notes: Branches are cheap pointers to commits — create one per feature or fix. Merge with `git merge` for a merge commit or `git rebase` for a linear history (never rebase shared branches).

languages.bash:
# Create a new branch and switch to it:
git checkout -b feature/login
# or: git switch -c feature/login

# List branches (* marks the current one):
git branch

# Switch branches:
git checkout main
# or: git switch main

# Merge a branch into the current branch:
git checkout main
git merge feature/login

# Delete a merged branch:
git branch -d feature/login

# Push the new branch to the remote:
git push -u origin feature/login

# Rename the current branch:
git branch -m new-name
# or: git branch -m old-name new-name   (renames any branch)

# Rename a branch and update the remote:
git branch -m old-name new-name
git push origin -u new-name
git push origin --delete old-name

tasks.intro: Here's how to stash and restore uncommitted work in Git.
tasks.notes: `git stash` is for when you must switch branches mid-work. `git stash pop` restores and removes the stash; use `git stash apply` if you want to keep it. Stashes are local — they never push.

languages.bash:
# Save uncommitted changes and clean the working tree:
git stash            # `git stash push -m "wip"` to label it

# See stashes:
git stash list

# Restore the latest stash and remove it:
git stash pop

# Restore without removing (keeps it for later):
git stash apply

# Drop a specific stash:
git stash drop stash@{0}

# Stash including untracked files:
git stash -u

tasks.intro: Here's how to inspect commit history with Git.
tasks.notes: `git log --oneline` gives a compact history; `--graph` shows branch topology. Add `--author`, `--since`, or `-S` to filter. `git log -p` shows the actual diffs.

languages.bash:
# Compact history (one line per commit):
git log --oneline

# With branch topology:
git log --oneline --graph --all

# Last 10 commits with diffs:
git log -p -10

# Commits by a specific author:
git log --author="alice"

# Commits touching a file:
git log --oneline -- src/main.py

# Search commit messages for a phrase:
git log --grep="fix" --oneline

tasks.intro: Here's how to work with files and directories from the {lang} command line.
tasks.notes: `find` is more powerful than `ls` for searching; `grep -r` searches inside files. `chmod` uses octal modes (755 = rwxr-xr-x) or symbolic ones (u+x). Always quote filenames with spaces.

languages.bash:
# List files (ls) / search (find):
ls -la
find . -name "*.py" -type f

# Search inside file contents:
grep -r "TODO" src/
grep -n "def main" main.py

# Copy / move / delete:
cp file.txt backup.txt
mv old.txt new.txt
rm file.txt            # ⚠️ no trash can — deletes permanently
rm -r directory/

# Permissions (octal: r=4, w=2, x=1):
chmod 755 script.sh     # rwxr-xr-x
chmod +x script.sh      # make executable
chown user:group file.txt

# Show file contents:
cat file.txt
less file.txt           # scrollable

tasks.intro: Here's how to make HTTP requests from the {lang} command line with curl.
tasks.notes: `curl -s` silences the progress meter, `-o` writes to a file, and `-X POST -d '...'` sends a request body. Add `-H 'Content-Type: application/json'` when posting JSON, and `-i` to see response headers.

languages.bash:
# GET (silent, show response body):
curl -s https://api.example.com/users

# GET with a query parameter:
curl -s "https://api.example.com/users?page=2"

# Show response headers too:
curl -si https://api.example.com/users

# POST JSON:
curl -s -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"name\": \"Alice\"}"

# Download to a file:
curl -s -o page.html https://example.com/

# Follow redirects:
curl -sL https://example.com

# Pretty-print JSON with jq:
curl -s https://api.example.com/users | jq .

tasks.intro: Here's how to pass arguments to a bash script.
tasks.notes: `$0` is the script name, `$1`…`$9` are positional args (use `${10}` for the tenth), `$@` is all args, `$#` is the count. Quote `"$@"` to preserve args with spaces. `shift` removes the first arg.

languages.bash:
#!/bin/bash
# Run as: ./script.sh alice 42

echo "script: $0"
echo "first arg: $1"
echo "second arg: $2"
echo "all args: $@"
echo "arg count: $#"

# Defaults for missing args:
NAME="${1:-world}"
AGE="${2:-unknown}"
echo "Hello $NAME ($AGE)"

# Loop over every arg:
for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "got: $arg"
done

# Use shift to process args one by one:
while [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; do
    echo "processing: $1"
    shift
done

tasks.intro: Here's how to rebase a branch onto main in git.
tasks.notes: Rebasing replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history. Only rebase commits you haven't pushed. Abort anytime with git rebase --abort.

languages.bash:
# Switch to your feature branch:
git checkout feature-branch

# Replay its commits onto main:
git rebase main

# If conflicts occur, resolve them, then:
git add <resolved-files>
git rebase --continue

# Or bail out entirely:
git rebase --abort

# One-liner from main:
git checkout main && git pull && git checkout feature-branch && git rebase main

# Interactive rebase (squash/reword/reorder):
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# After rebasing a pushed branch, force-push:
git push --force-with-lease

tasks.intro: Here's how to cherry-pick a commit in git.
tasks.notes: cherry-pick applies one commit's changes onto your current branch — useful for moving a hotfix without merging the whole branch. Copy the commit hash from git log.

languages.bash:
# Find the commit hash:
git log --oneline -10

# Apply it to the current branch:
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

# Cherry-pick without committing yet:
git cherry-pick -n a1b2c3d

# Multiple commits in order:
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d e4f5a6b

# A range of commits:
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d..e4f5a6b

# If it conflicts, resolve, git add, then:
git cherry-pick --continue

# Or abandon the operation:
git cherry-pick --abort

tasks.intro: Here's how to resolve a merge conflict in git.
tasks.notes: Conflicted files get conflict markers: <<<<<<< (yours), ======= (divider), >>>>>>> (theirs). Edit to the final content, git add, and commit. Use git mergetool for a visual diff.

languages.bash:
# When a merge/rebase/pull reports conflicts:
git status          # lists 'both modified' files

# Open the file and resolve the markers:
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# your version
# =======
# their version
# >>>>>>> feature-branch

# Keep yours / theirs wholesale:
git checkout --ours file.txt
git checkout --theirs file.txt

# After editing:
git add file.txt
git commit           # merge: creates the merge commit
git rebase --continue  # if you were rebasing

# Visual tool:
git mergetool

# Abort the whole merge:
git merge --abort

tasks.intro: Here's how to amend the last commit in git.
tasks.notes: git commit --amend replaces the last commit's message (and can add staged changes). Only amend commits you haven't pushed — otherwise force-push with --force-with-lease.

languages.bash:
# Change only the message:
git commit --amend -m 'new message'

# Add forgotten changes to the last commit:
git add forgotten.py
git commit --amend --no-edit    # keep the same message

# Edit the message in your editor:
git commit --amend

# Author too:
git commit --amend --author='alice <alice@example.com>'

# If already pushed, force-push carefully:
git push --force-with-lease

tasks.intro: Here's how to squash commits in git.
tasks.notes: git rebase -i HEAD~n opens an editor listing the last n commits; change 'pick' to 'squash' (or 's') on all but the first line to merge them into it. The first commit keeps its message unless you reword it. Only squash commits you haven't pushed.

languages.bash:
# Squash the last 3 commits into one:
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# In the editor that opens, keep 'pick' on the first line and
# change the other lines from 'pick' to 'squash':
#   pick  1a2b3c4 feat: add auth
#   squash 5d6e7f8 wip
#   squash 9a0b1c2 fix review comments

# Then edit the combined commit message and save.
# Verify the result:
git log --oneline

tasks.intro: Here's how to find the commit that broke something with git bisect.
tasks.notes: git bisect start, mark the current commit bad and an old commit good, then bisect checks out the midpoint for you to test. Answer 'good'/'bad' each round; bisect narrows to the culprit in log2(n) steps. End with git bisect reset.

languages.bash:
# Start:
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # current commit is broken
git bisect good <old-commit>  # a known-good commit

# Bisect checks out a midpoint — test it, then:
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad

# When it names the culprit, clean up:
git bisect reset

tasks.intro: Here's how to use git worktree.
tasks.notes: git worktree add <path> <branch> checks out another branch in a separate directory — no stashing or switching needed. Each worktree shares the same repo; list them with git worktree list and remove with git worktree remove.

languages.bash:
# Check out a branch in a separate directory:
git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch

# List all worktrees:
git worktree list

# Remove when done:
git worktree remove ../hotfix
